Monolithic kernels run scheduling, memory management, file systems, device drivers, and networking in one privileged address space with direct function calls.
Linux and traditional Unix use monolithic kernels for speed.
A faulty driver can crash an entire monolithic system, and a monolithic kernel is too large to easily prove correct.
Microkernels usually retain scheduling, basic memory protection, and messaging in kernel space while file systems, drivers, and networking run in user space.
Minix, QNX, and seL4 are microkernel examples.
A user-space driver can fail without crashing a microkernel system, and some microkernels have been formally verified.
Microkernel messaging incurs more overhead than direct function calls and can make a system slower than Linux.
macOS uses a hybrid kernel with many services retained in kernel space for speed.

Monolithic kernels run process management, memory management, drivers, file systems, and other services in the same privileged space, reducing communication overhead.
A bug or vulnerability in one monolithic component can crash or compromise the entire system.
Microkernels retain scheduling, inter-process communication, and low-level memory protection in the kernel while drivers, file systems, and networking run as separate user-space processes.
Microkernels improve fault isolation, modularity, and maintenance but can incur greater communication overhead.
Monolithic kernels favor speed and simplicity, while microkernels favor reliability, extensibility, and safer system design.
